topic: Expert C++ Implementation Concept: Overload Resolution and Reference Collapsing
explanation: This example highlights the intricate details of C++ overload resolution, specifically focusing on how the compiler handles references, reference collapsing, and the impact on function selection.  Understanding this requires knowledge of how the compiler performs name lookup, implicit conversions, and the nuances of reference parameters.  Performance implications are subtle, primarily impacting function call overhead and potential register allocation, but the core issue lies in compile-time behavior and potential ambiguity.
syntax: C++ function overloading with lvalue and rvalue references, const correctness
code_example: int f(const int &x) { std::cout << "f(const int&)"; return x + 1; }
int f(int &x) { std::cout << "f(int&)"; x = x * 2; return x; }
int g(const int &x) { std::cout << "g(const int&)"; return x + 10; }
int g(int x) { std::cout << "g(int)"; return x - 5; }
int j = f(i); // calls f(int &) -  lvalue reference is preferred over const lvalue reference.
int k = g(i); // ambiguous, compiler error - both overloads are equally viable.
//int l = g(5); // calls g(int) - rvalue passed, implicit conversion
//int m = f(5); //ambiguous - needs to distinguish between int&& and const int&
example_explanation: The compiler's overload resolution mechanism considers the types and qualifiers of arguments during compile time.  In `f(i)`,  `i` is an lvalue, so the `f(int&)` overload is preferred over `f(const int&)`, even though an implicit conversion to `const int&` is possible.  This preference stems from the compiler's attempt to avoid unnecessary copies and const-ness constraints.  The `g(i)` call is ambiguous because both overloads are equally viable without explicit type conversions. The compiler cannot determine which overload to choose, resulting in a compile-time error.  At the assembly level, the selected function's prologue and epilogue would be generated. This includes stack frame setup, parameter passing (pass-by-reference involves passing the address), and return value handling.  The difference between passing by value and by reference is primarily observed in the way the arguments are passed (address vs. value) which significantly impacts both stack usage and performance for large objects.  If `g(i)` were unambiguous, the choice of overload might impact instruction count and register usage depending on the compiler's optimization strategy.  The use of const references prevents modification of the original object, potentially improving code safety and, in some contexts, enabling compiler optimizations.
